interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is that two amounts in proportion make a straight line through (0, 0), so doubling the reading along doubles the reading up, while a line that misses (0, 0), or bends, is not in proportion, and that with voltage up the side a steeper V-I line means more ohms, when you draw a resistor's V-I graph from V = IR, test lines for proportion, compare resistors' lines, swap the axes and judge measured readings.
interactive.title: Straight lines through zero
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. Each shows a graph whose axes are named with their units: resistors' voltage against current, a call-out bill against hours, a cable drum's weight against its cable, a heater's power against its current and a tank's level against time. Lines and curves are drawn from their rules or from example readings, and a reading cursor runs up from the bottom axis to the line and across to the side. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it.
interactive.ignores: All the amounts are example values, chosen so the numbers come out simply: the resistors' ohms, the call-out's £40 and £30 an hour, the drum's 20 kg and 0.5 kg a metre, the 5 Ω heater, the part's curve, the tank's level and the measured readings. The resistors and the heater are taken to keep the same resistance at every current, though a real one's changes as it warms, and the part's bent V-I curve is drawn from example numbers, not from a real component. Steepness is compared by eye only; working it out as a number comes in a later course.

A 5 Ω heater by P = I²R: 2² × 5 = 20 W at 2 A and 4² × 5 = 80 W at 4 A, four times as much, in step 5
An example part's V-I curve through (0, 0), (2, 5), (4, 15) and (6, 30): 15 V at 4 A, not 2 × 5 = 10 V or 4 × 5 = 20 V, in step 6

explain.text:
Two amounts are in direct proportion when doubling one doubles the other and 0 goes with 0, as in Proportional reasoning. On a graph, that is a straight line through (0, 0). A resistor's voltage and current work this way, as long as its resistance stays the same. By V = IR, a 5 Ω resistor takes 5 V at 1 A, 10 V at 2 A and 20 V at 4 A, and 0 V at 0 A, so its points lie on one straight line through (0, 0). BBC Bitesize says that when the V-I graph is a straight line that passes through the origin, the current and voltage are proportional.[^1] So along such a line, doubling the current doubles the voltage. A resistor reading 6 V at 2 A reads 12 V at 4 A, not 8 V.

Both parts of the test matter. A £40 call-out plus £30 an hour makes a straight line, but it starts at £40, so 4 hours cost £160, not double the £100 for 2 hours. A 5 Ω heater's power, by P = I²R, starts at (0, 0) but curves upwards, from 20 W at 2 A to 80 W at 4 A, four times as much. A V-I line can bend too: OpenStax notes that if it is not straight, the material is not ohmic, so Ohm's law cannot be used for it.[^2] Read where the axes start, too, since a line running into a corner marked 20 cm misses (0, 0). With voltage up the side, RMIT calls R the slope of the V-I graph,[^3] so on the same axes a [[steeper]] line means more ohms, and a 10 Ω line climbs twice as steeply as a 5 Ω one. Bitesize draws voltage on the y-axis and current on the x-axis,[^4] as most of this lesson does, but books differ and some put current up the side. Then the 5 Ω line is the steeper one, so read the axis labels first.

**Two amounts are in proportion when their graph is a straight line through (0, 0), like a resistor's V-I graph from V = IR. A line that misses (0, 0), or bends, is not in proportion. With voltage up the side, a steeper V-I line on the same axes means more ohms, but read the axis labels first, as some books swap them.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** To test a graph for proportion, check that the line is straight and that it passes through (0, 0), reading where each axis starts. If both hold, doubling one amount doubles the other. On a V-I graph, read the axis labels before you judge steepness.

**Worked example:** A resistor reads 6 V at 2 A, and its V-I graph is a straight line through (0, 0). At 4 A, double the current, it reads 2 × 6 = 12 V. By V = IR it is a 3 Ω resistor, and 4 × 3 = 12 V checks it.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking any straight line as proportional. A cable drum weighing 20 kg empty plus 0.5 kg a metre makes a straight line, but it misses (0, 0), so 40 m of cable weighs 40 kg, not twice the 30 kg of 20 m.
- Taking a line from (0, 0) that bends as proportional. A part whose V-I line is not straight is not ohmic,[^2] so read its voltage off the curve rather than doubling.
- Taking the corner as (0, 0). If the side starts at 20 cm, a line from the corner starts at 20 cm, not 0.
- Judging steepness without the labels. With voltage up the side a steeper line on the same axes means more ohms,[^3] but with current up the side the steeper line has fewer.
- Joining measured readings dot to dot. Lay one best-fit line through them, as in From a table to a graph, and see whether it runs through (0, 0), or very close to it, since readings wobble a little.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is that two amounts in proportion make a straight line through (0, 0), so doubling the reading along doubles the reading up, while a line that misses (0, 0), or bends, is not in proportion, and that with voltage up the side a steeper V-I line means more ohms, when you draw a resistor's V-I graph from V = IR, test lines for proportion, compare resistors' lines, swap the axes and judge measured readings.

checks.label: The V-I graph is a straight line that passes through the origin, this shows that the current and voltage are proportional: every resistor line drawn from V = IR (3, 4, 5, 8 and 10 Ω) passes through (0, 0), and along each, doubling the current doubles the voltage, so 6 V at 2 A is 12 V at 4 A

If the line were not straight, then the material would not be ohmic and we would not be able to use Ohm's law: the example part's V-I curve bends, its volts per amp going from 2.5 at 2 A to 3.75 at 4 A, so no one resistance fits it and doubling 2 A gives 15 V, not 10 V

R (the slope of the V-I graph) is a constant for a given conductor and is called the resistance: with voltage up the side each resistor's line climbs R volts for every amp, so the steeper line is the one with more ohms; the 10 Ω line is drawn steeper than the 5 Ω, and line B (8 Ω) is the steepest of A (4 Ω), B and C (3 Ω)

With voltage on the y-axis and current on the x-axis: every V-I graph in the lesson puts voltage up the side, except the screens that say they have current up the side; when the axes swap, the 5 Ω line ends at (30, 6) and is steeper than the 10 Ω line ending at (30, 3), and with current up the side the line that climbs less (line B, 15 Ω, 2 A at 30 V, against line A, 6 Ω, 5 A at 30 V) has more ohms

A line that misses (0, 0) or bends is not in proportion, worked from each rule: the call-out costs £100 for 2 h and £160 for 4 h, not £200; the drum weighs 20 kg at 0 m, 30 kg at 20 m and 40 kg at 40 m, not 60 kg; the heater gives 20 W at 2 A and 80 W at 4 A, four times; the tank holds 20 cm at 0 min and 50 cm at 6 min

Each puzzle's answer is worked out from its rule: (4, 12); it misses (0, 0); 15 V; line B; (6, 2) for 3 Ω at 2 A, current up; line B, the one with more ohms, current up; the tank misses (0, 0), its side starting at 20 cm; and the measured readings' best-fit line runs within half a square of every reading, through (0, 0), with some above it and some below

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, and each wrong answer it names is the one a slip gives: 2 added instead of doubling, the voltage kept, the curve's reading doubled or made four times, a line that runs furthest or is flattest, voltage put up the side, the ohms added to the amps, the steeper line taken as more ohms with current up the side; each straight, corner and zigzag slip is shown in the warning colour

Before an answer, nothing in a puzzle's picture gives it away: no line through the given point, no answer point or reading, the drag point's readout says (?, ?), no line's ohms, the side not redrawn from 0, no best-fit line, nothing in the warning colour
Every screen, finished, keeps its labels inside the picture and clear of each other and its points inside the graph, for every answer, right or wrong, and wherever the reading is slid

Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s and a slip within 1 s; parts start at least 0.45 s apart and counted steps at least 0.2 s apart

applied.problem: Steepness only shows ohms when lines share the same axes and scales; a resistor is proportional only while its resistance holds; the heater's bend sat beside 'not ohmic' as if linked; screens 9-10 put current up the side, so not the whole lesson follows Bitesize.

Comparing steepness needs the same axes and scales, and a best-fit line through real measured readings rarely passes exactly through (0, 0), so asking only whether it runs through (0, 0) would wrongly reject proportional data.
The 5 Ω heater is also drawn with a fixed resistance, but a real heater element's resistance changes as it warms; ignores names only the resistors as held constant.

notes.problem: Every number (the ohms, the £40 and £30, the drum, heater, part, tank and the measured readings) is an example value chosen for the lesson, as ignores says, so its kind is "assumed" (or "computed" from its rule), not "constant".
